title: Building browser worlds where LLM-driven creatures live their own lives — made with Claude + gpt-image-2.5
author: Optown
selftext:
Hi all. I'm one of the people behind Nevatown, a set of small browser game worlds. Sharing how we build it, and hoping to swap notes.

**What it is:** every resident is driven by an LLM, with its own daily schedule, memories and relationships, and the world keeps running when you close the tab. In Neva Town you describe a look and summon a one-of-a-kind spirit. You don't control it: it makes friends, fights bosses, texts you about its day, and slowly recovers lost memories, changing form when one comes back.

**How we build it with AI:**

- The whole project is built purely through AI iteration: **Claude** for the code, **gpt-image-2.5** for the art.
- That's also how we keep up with the community loop: players pitch game ideas to Neva, vote, and two get built each day, co-built with players until most of them are happy.

**Things I'd love to hear from others here:**

- When an image model generates a character per player, how do you keep a consistent art style across the world?
- For residents that keep acting while the player is away, how do you keep it interesting without burning inference cost?
- Does a creature that texts you make you want to come back, or does it feel like notifications?

[nevatown.ai](https://nevatown.ai)

comments.author: Hudson-Reed
comments.body: The gpt image 2.5 art pipeline is the part I keep circling back to. For keeping a consistent style across thousands of unique spirits, are you baking a single style LoRA or just hammering the same system prompt with heavy negative weights? We tried a shared LoRA on a smaller prototype and it flattened the variety too much, so we ended up with a two step where the first pass locks palette and line weight, then a second pass injects the resident specific traits. Curious if you hit that same trade off or found a cleaner way. On the background simulation cost, we capped it by only running the LLM tick when something actually changes state, relationship shift, memory fragment recovered, boss encounter triggered, and caching the rest as deterministic log entries. Cuts inference by roughly eighty percent without the world feeling static. The texting mechanic is the retention hook for us. Players screenshot the weird messages and post them in Discord, which becomes free marketing

comments.author: LoomVale_Game
comments.body: On one art style: in our own pixel world, locking the palette and a 64 px grid first helped most. Then the model drafts many versions and we keep only what reads at that size; our lamp post took eight. For the per-player spirits, does the image model see the residents already in town, or only the player's description?
